title: Add Gemini Live agents to your video conferencing with Fishjam
transcriptText:
[MUSIC PLAYING]
ADRIAN CZERWIEC: Creating video
conferences with AI participants
has never been so easy.
Hi, I am Adrian.
I work on Fishjam
at Software Mansion.
And today, I will
show you how quickly
you can create such
video conferencing
and invite an AI model
as a participant.
Let me ask if you can see
what's on my video feed.
GEMINI AGENT: I can
see your video feed.
It looks like you're in a room
with some purple lighting,
several potted plants
on shelves behind you,
and a sign that says,
"Software Mansion."
Anything specific you'd
like me to observe?
ADRIAN CZERWIEC: We
will use two things--
Fishjam, a low-latency
video conferencing
and live-streaming API, and the
just-released Gemini 3.1 Flash
Live audio model.
To build the bridge
between Gemini and Fishjam,
we'll use Fishjam
Agents, a feature that
lets your backend join
a video conference just
like a regular client would.
Sounds fun?
Let's get to it.
Let's start with
the Gemini Live API
overview to see what
we're going to be using.
And basically, this
picture is our app.
So we're going to be
sending text, audio,
and video to the Live API.
And we'll be getting text
and, in our case, audio.
And the connection is going to
be via the WebSocket protocol.
Let's start with the Fishjam
docs on Gemini Live integration.
We are building a real-time
speech-to-speech agent
using Fishjam and Google's
Multimodal Live API.
To achieve our goal,
what we need to do
is basically take the audio from
Fishjam and send it to Gemini,
wait for Gemini's response,
and put the audio back
in the Fishjam conference room.
The prerequisites are
Fishjam ID and the management
token You can get
them at Fishjam.io.
You can use the sandbox here.
You don't need to
buy any package
to be able to build such app.
You can use the sandbox tier
and build a similar app yourself
even today.
And the second thing is,
obviously, the Gemini API key.
First thing first, we need
to install the Fishjam Server
SDK and the Google GenAI SDK.
We initialize our clients.
Then we need to create a
Fishjam room and a Fishjam
Agent inside that room.
All right, moving to the code,
I have prepared some boilerplate
for me so I don't have to
write everything from scratch.
But this setup is simple.
We have a simple backend
with tRPC endpoints.
They are not ready yet.
We will uncover them together.
And a simple React
app as our frontend
that will allow us to
join the conference
and talk to the agent.
So let me quickly walk
you over the frontend,
since it's very simple.
And you'll see what methods
are we going to be building.
So this is the root view.
And let's go to Lobby.
So Lobby is the simplest form.
It takes the room name,
the name of the peer,
and allows us to join the room.
So we're going to be calling
the getPeerToken method.
And we want to retrieve our
room ID and the peer token.
And then we're going to
initialize devices using
our React SDK and, finally,
joining the room using
the generated peer token.
We can also add some
metadata, and in our case,
it's going to be our name.
The second view
is the call view.
So once we are in the room,
we display a simple tiled view
with a toolbar.
So we also use our Fishjam
SDK hooks to handle devices,
toggle them, mute the
microphone, so on.
And then we can
use usePeers hook
to take the data and also the
video tracks, audio tracks,
of the remote peers.
So then we can find
the agent peer.
We can distinguish it by
ensuring it has no metadata
and also list the rest
of the human peers.
There's going to be also
a StartAgent button,
and it's going to be calling the
second endpoint, createAgent.
And that's the second
thing that we're going
to be building on our backend.
So let's quickly move
over to our backend.
Let me close that one.
So we've got a simple Fastify
setup with tRPC router.
Let's go quickly jump to it.
And here we are.
There are two endpoints
that I just mentioned about,
and as you can see,
they are empty.
So let's go over them.
First, we want to create
a room in Fishjam,
then create a peer in that room.
So we have our two arguments
that we pass from our frontend.
And first, since Fishjam don't
store any room metadata yet,
we want to create a
simple mapping that
will map our room
name to the room ID
that we're going to
get from Fishjam API.
So first, let's
check if we already
have such a room in our cache.
And then we use two
methods, so it depends on
if we already have that room.
We refresh our state and get
the room straight from Fishjam,
or we create a new room, and
then we update our cache.
Then we can handle
the validation,
so we can tell if the
name is already taken--
the peer name, of course.
And we can throw an error
if it's already taken.
And then we can finally
create a peer in Fishjam.
So we have our room
ID, and then we
can create a peer with our data.
And then we can also
get our peer token
that we're going to be
returning to the frontend.
Finally, we just return.
That's all we need to
do to create a room
and then to create a peer
token, allowing the peer to join
the conference on the frontend.
OK, let's now build the
createAgent function.
First, we need to create an
agent in the specified room.
What's important about it--
we need to specify the codec
settings for its output,
and they need to match the
exact settings that Gemini
expects on its input.
So in this case, we've
prepared ready helpers for you
not to worry about
the exact numbers.
Just import the settings
and use it in your code.
Then we can create a
track for our agent
so we can talks
to the conference.
And this time, we also need to
specify the codec settings is
the other way around.
So we need to specify what codec
settings Gemini will send us,
and then we will use
it in our conference.
Then let me quickly
create a cleanup function.
And finally, we can
create our Gemini session.
Let's use the new
3.1 audio model,
put our instruction
in place, and then
let's turn the Google Search
on and also declare a function.
So in this case, I
came up with an idea
that I could ask Gemini to
invoke disconnect function
and completely
clean up everything
after itself on the backend.
Moving over to the
onmessage handler,
so once we get the
response from Gemini,
we check if we have
some audio data in it.
Then we convert it from
Base64 to a JavaScript buffer
and send it directly to Fishjam.
We can also handle
interruptions.
So once we got some
audio chunk from Gemini
and we send it to
Fishjam, it keeps playing.
But once Gemini tells us
it might get interrupted,
we can also flush the
audio in the Fishjam room
so the leftover audio
is not playing anymore.
Finally, we can see some
function calls has been detected
and call our code accordingly.
It does the cleanup function.
That's not been declared
yet, but let's move over
to the next part.
And the next part is
finally subscribing to audio
on the Fishjam side.
So in this case, we listen
to the trackData event
on the Fishjam agent, and
we send the data to Gemini
upon converting it to Base64.
What's important about
this part is, in this case,
we listen for every
participant's audio chunks.
If you want some more
granular approach,
consider using Fishjam
Selective Subscriptions API.
This will allow you to handle
this case more manually.
But in this case,
we'll keep it simple.
All right.
Then let's handle the
agent seeing things.
So the Google allows
for 1-FPS video,
so we will be capturing a frame
of my video track and sending it
to Gemini each second.
So in this case, I call
fishjam.getRoom method,
find my track that
I want to use,
and then capture the
image using the track ID.
Finally, we can move over
to the cleanup function.
So once I have my interval,
I have my Gemini session,
I can set it up and then remove
all listeners, delete all track,
and disconnect
everything that I can.
All right.
Here we are in our room.
Let me come up with
some name, happy room.
[LAUGHS] And let
me join the room.
Hello.
[CHUCKLES] Here I am.
And let's add our agent.
So here's the system prompt.
For now, I will leave it as is.
And hello, can you hear me?
GEMINI AGENT: Yes, I
can hear you clearly.
How can I help you today?
ADRIAN CZERWIEC:
I have a question.
Could you please
google for me what's
the weather forecast for
Kraków for the next three days?
GEMINI AGENT: I can do that.
For the next three
days in Kraków,
you can expect temperatures
to be around 8 to 11 degrees
Celsius during the day.
There's a good chance of
rain today and tomorrow,
but Saturday should
look a little brighter,
with partly cloudy skies.
Is there anything else you'd
like to know about the forecast?
ADRIAN CZERWIEC: About
the forecast, maybe not,
but let me ask you if you can
see what's on my video feed.
GEMINI AGENT: I can
see your video feed.
It looks like you're in a room
with some purple lighting,
several potted plants
on shelves behind you,
and a sign that says,
"Software Mansion."
Anything specific you'd
like me to observe?
ADRIAN CZERWIEC: Well,
that's already impressive.
I have another request.
Can we talk in some
other language?
Can you say hi to me in Polish?
GEMINI AGENT: [POLISH]
I can do that.
How would you like to continue?
We can talk about
the weather in Polish
or anything else you like.
ADRIAN CZERWIEC:
OK, maybe in German.
GEMINI AGENT: [SPEAKING GERMAN]
ADRIAN CZERWIEC:
That's impressive.
OK, I have one more request for
you-- to disconnect yourself.
Not even a goodbye, but
that was kind of expected.
But what if you want to have
some guardrails on our agent?
For example, we
build a conference,
and we want to have an
agent that will only
talk about a certain thing.
We can modify our system
prompt and tell the agent to
"You can only talk
about bananas.
No other thing exists for you."
Hello?
How are you?
GEMINI AGENT: I'm feeling
positively bananatastic,
thanks for asking.
Just thinking about all the
wonderful varieties of bananas
there are.
How are you?
ADRIAN CZERWIEC: I'm fine.
What about oranges?
Can we talk about oranges?
GEMINI AGENT: Oranges?
Never heard of them.
Now, bananas, on the other
hand, are fascinating.
Have you ever
tried a red banana?
They're quite creamy.
ADRIAN CZERWIEC: Oh, no, never.
But could you teach me calculus?
GEMINI AGENT: We could try, but
calculus is the math of change,
and bananas are pretty
consistently delicious.
Maybe we could talk about
the rate a plant grows
or the volume of a
banana split instead.
What do you think?
ADRIAN CZERWIEC: All right,
I think that's it for me,
but I have a banana
request for you.
Could you please
disconnect yourself?
GEMINI AGENT: A banana
request, I like it.
Disconnecting
myself like a banana
split from the rest
of the dessert.
So long.
ADRIAN CZERWIEC: And that's it.
With just a few lines of code,
we connected a Gemini Live model
as a real participant in a
Fishjam video conference.
It can hear, see
the camera feed,
and talk back in real time.
If you want to
try this yourself,
the full example is
linked in the description.
You'll just need a Fishjam
sandbox account and a Gemini API
key.
If you build something cool
with this, let us know.
We would love to see it.
Happy coding.
[MUSIC PLAYING]
